newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - RENAULT SHUTS BELGIAN PLANT AFTER LOSS.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - RENAULT SHUTS BELGIAN PLANT AFTER LOSS.

text.p: French car maker Renault announced a major reorganisation of production on Thursday after admitting it made a loss in 1996 for the first time in 10 years.

Renault said it would reduce the number of its European production sites to 12 with the closure in July of its Belgian plant at Vilvoorde, near Brussels, moving its production of Megane and Clio models to sites in France and Spain.

In a statement outlining the closure, Renault said 1996 results would be "significantly negative". France's Les Echos newspaper reported the loss could be four to five billion francs ($709 to $887 million). The company declined to comment.
"The accounts are not consolidated yet. We can make no comment before March 20" when the company is due to announce its results, a Renault spokeswoman said.

The Belgian factory's closure and associated reorganisation would allow the group to produce its five flagship models - Safrane, Laguna, Megane, Clio and Twingo - at eight sites, rather than the 12 presently used.
"Assuming that we maintain the same level of output...this will save us 850 million (French) francs a year," she said.
The news shocked the 3,100 strong Belgian workforce, coming just days after some received merit awards from Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who lives in Vilvoorde.
"This was not expected," a spokesman for Renault Industrie Belgique told Reuters, summing up the workers' disbelief.
"The personnel feel deceived," Metal Working Union (CMB) Secretary General Karel Gacoms told RTBF television. "We cannot accept this closure and the way it has been carried out."
Key production areas were blockaded and finished cars awaiting shipping stopped from leaving the factory. Further union action was to be outlined on Friday.
Dehaene said he was dismayed by the "brutal and unilateral decision of the French management of Renault" to close the factory.
"Renault Vilvoorde risks becoming a victim of a strategic decision ... which takes no account of the social repercussions on the area," he said in a statement.
The Flemish regional government said it was "stunned and disappointed".
The closure is likely to send shivers through the Belgian economy, which also boasts major Ford, Opel and Volvo car plants.
Renault said it would look for another manufacturer to take over its Belgian plant, which produced 143,342 cars in 1996. The spokeswoman said, however, that no talks were under way.
The workforce at its other plants would rise by the "equivalent" of 1,900 of the Vilvoorde workers but there were no plans to offer Belgians jobs at other Renault plants, the spokeswoman added.

Renault, hit by sluggish sales and a savage price war, reported a 41 percent drop in 1995 net attributable profit to 2.14 billion francs. First-half profits slid to 158 million francs from 1.76 billion a year earlier.
Renault shares, which had been losing ground amid deepening gloom over the carmaker's outlook, rebounded on rumours of the plant closure, closing up 4.92 percent at 130.0 francs.
